summary: Defines a Transport Subsystem for the SNMP architecture, a place for Transport Models comparable to the other subsystems in the SNMP architecture of RFC 3411. It makes it possible to run SNMP over transports beyond UDP, including secure ones.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds a transport component to the SNMP architecture. It lets different transport models carry SNMP messages and pass relevant transport-security information to the parts of SNMP that need it.

questions: what is the snmp transport subsystem

how does snmp use ssh or tls
subtitle: An SNMP architecture component that lets pluggable transport models carry management messages.

tldr.problem: The SNMP architecture had no subsystem for transport models, including secure transports that provide their own authentication or encryption. Operators also wanted to use security infrastructure shared with other management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Transport Subsystem, sendMessage and receiveMessage interfaces, and a tmStateReference cache for passing transport and security information between SNMP subsystems.
tldr.outcome: Transport models can be designed separately and can use secure transports such as SSH or TLS. RFC 5590 updates RFC 3411, RFC 3412, RFC 3414, and RFC 3417.

today: RFC 5590 is an Internet Standard and updates RFC 3411, RFC 3412, RFC 3414, and RFC 3417. The RFC describes Transport Security and Secure Shell Transport Models in RFC 5591 and RFC 5592.

sections.title: Why SNMP Needs a Transport Subsystem
sections.content:
The User-based Security Model (USM) provides Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) security with its own identities and key-management infrastructure. The RFC says operators found maintaining another such infrastructure a deterrent to deploying SNMP version 3 (SNMPv3) and wanted to reuse existing user-management systems.

Another approach is to let a lower-layer protocol provide security services. The RFC defines an architectural extension so SNMP can use transport models based on protocols such as Transport Layer Security (TLS) or Secure Shell (SSH), while leaving each transport model modular and independently extensible.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP already had its own security model, but operators wanted to use security systems they had for other management tools. The new subsystem gives those secure transports a place in the SNMP architecture.

sections.title: Where the Transport Subsystem Fits
sections.content:
RFC 3411 defines SNMP subsystems for dispatching, message processing, security, and access control. RFC 5590 adds a Transport Subsystem that contains Transport Models such as UDP, TCP, SSH, and TLS. Models can be added and standardized independently.

A secure transport can authenticate or encrypt a message before the Message Processing Model decodes it. Some security processing may then be repeated by the selected SNMP Security Model. A transport session may carry multiple SNMP messages, although the architecture does not define SNMP sessions or let the transport subsystem inspect the PDU type.
sections.plainLanguage: The Transport Subsystem sits between the SNMP engine and the network. It holds separate transport models, including models that provide security before an SNMP message is processed.

sections.title: Requirements for Transport Models
sections.content:
A transport security protocol should protect against message changes, impersonation, changes in message order, and disclosure. It should not make denial of service or traffic analysis significantly worse. A Transport Model should avoid changing the underlying protocol, and multiple Transport Models must be able to coexist.

A Transport Model may suggest a securityName and securityLevel, but the Security Model decides whether to use them. A new transport domain must define a prefix of one to four US-ASCII letters or digits, followed by a colon, so applications can distinguish identities authenticated by different transports.

A model may provide stronger security than requested, but must not downgrade the requested security level. If it cannot meet the requested level, it should discard the message and report the failure.
sections.plainLanguage: A transport model must meet the security level requested by SNMP and may provide stronger protection. It must not silently provide weaker protection or prevent another transport model from coexisting.

sections.title: The tmStateReference Cache
sections.content:
The tmStateReference identifies an implementation-specific cache of transport information. A transport model and a transport-aware Security Model use it to pass information without changing the wire format of SNMP messages.

A complete conceptual cache contains seven fields: tmTransportDomain, tmTransportAddress, tmSecurityName, tmRequestedSecurityLevel, tmTransportSecurityLevel, tmSameSecurity, and tmSessionID. These fields distinguish the transport identity and protection from the SNMP security identity and requested protection.

If a security model requires a response to use the same secure session as the request, the session identifier must still match when sending the response. Otherwise, the transport model must discard the response and report a send failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The cache carries transport details that the SNMP message itself may not contain. It lets later SNMP components check who the transport authenticated and what protection the session provided.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving SNMP Messages
sections.content:
RFC 5590 defines two Abstract Service Interfaces (ASIs) between the Dispatcher and Transport Subsystem. sendMessage passes an outgoing message, its destination transport domain and address, its length, and a transport-state reference. receiveMessage passes an incoming message and its source transport details in the other direction.

The RFC also adds transport-state references to existing outgoing and incoming interfaces. The Transport Model does not choose the Security Model for an incoming message; the Message Processing Model makes that decision after receiving the message.
sections.plainLanguage: One interface sends an SNMP message to a transport model, and another passes a received message back to the Dispatcher. The reference parameter carries transport state between the components.

sections.title: Security Model Compatibility
sections.content:
Each proposed Transport Model should explain its security properties, denial-of-service behavior, and whether perfect forward secrecy is appropriate. Implementations should protect the cache because it contains security-related information, and an SNMP engine must use credentials that it is permitted to use for a given user.

The RFC does not recommend pairing a secure transport with a Security Model that cannot use transport identity. Older models such as SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and USM may make access-control decisions using identities from the SNMP message rather than the identity authenticated by the transport.

The RFC recommends provisioning authenticated and encrypted USM as a fallback when a secure transport depends on external services that may be unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: A secure transport does not automatically make an older SNMP security model use the transport's identity. The cache and its credentials also need protection, and the RFC recommends a fallback that does not depend on external services.

sections.title: Transport Domain Names
sections.content:
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) created the SNMP Transport Domains registry. Each entry provides a one-to-four-character US-ASCII alphanumeric prefix for a transport domain and has an object identifier under snmpDomains. New entries use the Specification Required policy.

The initial prefixes listed by the RFC are udp, clns, cons, ddp, ipx, and prxy.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry assigns short prefixes to SNMP transport domains. Those names help SNMP identify which transport model applies.
